description: How to use buildings, parish registers, newspapers and oral history as evidence for the historic environment paper.
content_html:
Why Source Skills Matter for Spitalfields

The historic environment examination at OCR asks you to use specific types of evidence about Spitalfields. You must be able to explain what different sources reveal about migration patterns, evaluate their usefulness, and compare two sources effectively. This lesson drills the five main evidence types: physical fabric (buildings and streets), parish and civil registers, contemporary visual evidence, written contemporary accounts, and oral history.

A key principle: every piece of evidence tells you something, but also conceals something. A parish register from Christ Church Spitalfields shows who was baptised, married or buried there, and can indicate the ethnic or national origin of parishioners through the spelling of names. But it only records those who used the Anglican church — Jewish, Nonconformist and later Muslim residents would not appear. Knowing both what a source shows and what it omits is essential for the highest marks.

Physical Fabric as Evidence

The built environment of Spitalfields is itself a primary source. The surviving Georgian terraces on Fournier Street date from the early eighteenth century and reflect the prosperity of Huguenot weavers who could afford substantial brick-built homes with large windows for their looms. The architectural quality of these houses — compare them with the much more modest buildings in adjacent courts — tells us about the relative wealth of the Huguenot community.

The Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building is the single most evidence-rich site in Spitalfields. Built as a Huguenot chapel in 1743, it became a Methodist chapel, then a synagogue (c.1897), then a mosque (1976). Its physical adaptations — changes to the interior, the addition of a minaret, the presence of Hebrew inscriptions still visible inside — provide direct evidence of the succession of communities. Students should know that multiple layers of evidence within a single building is itself historically significant.

Key Fact

Five evidence types for Spitalfields: (1) Physical fabric — surviving buildings, street layouts; (2) Parish/civil registers — Christ Church records from 1729; (3) Contemporary visual evidence — Charles Booth poverty maps (1889), weaver portraits; (4) Written contemporary accounts — Henry Mayhew’s East End journalism (1860s); (5) Oral history — BBC Jewish East End recordings, Tower Hamlets Local History Library.

Documentary Sources: Registers and Surveys

Charles Booth’s poverty maps (1889 onwards) provide an invaluable visual record of social conditions in Spitalfields at the height of Jewish migration. Booth colour-coded streets from black (lowest class, semi-criminal) to yellow (wealthy). Streets in Spitalfields showed mixed conditions, with the poorest workers concentrated in courts off Brick Lane. The maps are quantified evidence of poverty levels but reflect Booth’s own assumptions — his descriptions of Jewish immigrants show both admiration for their industry and Victorian prejudices about class.

Henry Mayhew’s journalism from the 1840s–1860s captured the street life of Spitalfields before the Jewish migration, describing Irish costermongers (street sellers) and the conditions of casual labourers. His accounts give voice to individuals who left no other written record, but are shaped by Mayhew’s middle-class perspective and journalistic purposes.

Oral history is particularly valuable for communities that were marginalised, illiterate in English, or whose experiences were not recorded by official institutions. BBC recordings of Jewish East End residents (late twentieth century) capture daily life in Spitalfields in ways no parish register could: Yiddish street culture, family memories of pogrom flight, and experiences of anti-semitism. Tower Hamlets Local History Library and Archives holds oral history recordings from the Bangladeshi community. These sources give insight into lived experience but have limitations: memory is selective, and retrospective accounts may be shaped by later events.

Key Fact

Source comparison structure: (1) What does each source show about migration? (2) How do they differ in perspective or purpose? (3) What does each source omit? (4) Which is more useful for understanding a specific aspect of Spitalfields history, and why? Always anchor your contextual knowledge to specific details about the site.

The 10-mark source comparison asks you to use two sources about Spitalfields and your own knowledge to explain how useful they are. A strong answer will: (a) make a direct comparison between the two sources (not treat them separately); (b) use specific details from each source; (c) deploy your own contextual knowledge about Spitalfields to confirm, challenge or extend what the sources suggest; (d) give a judgement on which source is more useful for the specific question asked, and why. Avoid summary (“Source A says... Source B says...”). Analyse and compare throughout.
exam_tip_html: For the 10-mark source comparison, the key skill is integration: compare the sources throughout your answer rather than treating each separately. Use Spitalfields-specific contextual knowledge (the Jamme Masjid building, Christ Church records from 1729, Booth’s poverty maps) to show why one or both sources are useful or limited. Examiners reward judgements about purpose and limitation — a parish register from Christ Church cannot show Jewish or Muslim settlement because those communities would not use an Anglican church. Saying this explicitly, and explaining why it matters, is what distinguishes a strong source-comparison answer.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five evidence types for Spitalfields: physical fabric (buildings, street layouts), parish and civil registers (Christ Church records from 1729), contemporary visual evidence (Booth’s poverty maps), written accounts (Mayhew’s journalism), and oral history (BBC Jewish East End recordings, Tower Hamlets Local History Library).
  • Every source has both revealing qualities and limitations: parish registers miss non-Anglican communities; oral history gives lived experience but memory is selective; Booth’s maps quantify poverty but carry Victorian assumptions.
  • The Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building is the most evidence-rich single site: its physical adaptations across four communities (Huguenot, Methodist, Jewish, Muslim) make it a layer-by-layer record of Spitalfields migration history.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Charles Booth's poverty maps as evidence for Spitalfields history.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the colour-coded maps (1889+) show poverty street by street, revealing the concentration of the poorest workers in courts off Brick Lane). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of parish registers as evidence for migration in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. Christ Church records from 1729 show names that indicate national origins; they can reveal patterns of settlement but omit non-Anglican communities) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Using your knowledge of Spitalfields, explain how oral history provides evidence that written records cannot.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation identifying specific oral history sources (BBC Jewish East End recordings, Tower Hamlets Bangladeshi community recordings) and explaining what they reveal (daily life, personal experience of prejudice, Yiddish culture) that parish registers and surveys do not capture, with reference to limitations of memory. Secure: Two or three specific examples with explanation. Developing: General reference to oral history without site-specific examples. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Using Sources A and B [supplied in exam] and your own knowledge, explain how useful these sources are for understanding migration in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, integrated comparison that uses specific details from both sources, deploys Spitalfields-specific contextual knowledge (naming specific buildings, dates, communities), evaluates both the usefulness and limitations of each source, and reaches a judgement on their relative value for the specific question. Secure: Clear comparison with some contextual knowledge and evaluation. Developing: Sources treated separately; some evaluation. Emerging: Describes sources without comparison or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the physical fabric of Spitalfields is particularly valuable as historical evidence for migration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation using specific examples (Jamme Masjid building's four uses, Fournier Street terraces, Christ Church) to show how physical fabric reveals migration patterns, economic status and community succession that documents alone cannot show, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with at least two specific examples. Developing: Some explanation with basic or generic evidence. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Henry Mayhew's journalism as evidence for life in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. detailed first-hand accounts of street sellers and casual labourers from 1840s–1860s; shaped by Mayhew's middle-class perspective which may distort working-class experience) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

knowledge_checks.q: From what year do documented parish records from Christ Church Spitalfields survive?
What does Charles Booth's poverty map use to show wealth and deprivation street by street?
A major limitation of Christ Church parish registers is that they only record _____ community members.
The Tower Hamlets Local History Library holds oral history recordings from the _____ community.
Match each source to what it is best at revealing about Spitalfields:
right: Daily life and personal experience of prejudice
Names and family origins of Anglican parishioners

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five types of evidence used for Spitalfields history.
flashcard_questions.a: Physical fabric, parish registers, contemporary visual evidence (Booth), written accounts (Mayhew), oral history

flashcard_questions.q: From what year do Christ Church Spitalfields parish records survive?
What is the key limitation of Christ Church parish registers for studying Spitalfields migration?
flashcard_questions.a: They only record Anglican parishioners — Jewish, Nonconformist and Muslim residents are invisible

flashcard_questions.q: What did Charles Booth's poverty maps (1889) show?
flashcard_questions.a: Colour-coded street-by-street poverty levels across London, including Spitalfields
Victorian journalist who documented East End street life in the 1840s–1860s

flashcard_questions.q: What is the advantage of oral history for Spitalfields research?
flashcard_questions.a: Captures daily life and lived experience that official records omit

flashcard_questions.q: What is the limitation of oral history?
flashcard_questions.a: Memory is selective; retrospective accounts may be shaped by later events

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building particularly valuable as evidence?
flashcard_questions.a: Its physical adaptations across four communities make it a direct record of migration succession

flashcard_questions.q: What does the quality of Fournier Street's Georgian terraces reveal?
flashcard_questions.a: The economic prosperity of the Huguenot weavers who built them

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key structure for a 10-mark source comparison?
flashcard_questions.a: Integrate sources throughout, use Spitalfields contextual knowledge, evaluate usefulness and limitations, give a judgement

glossary_terms.definition: A systematic record kept by a church recording baptisms, marriages and burials in a parish, providing evidence of who lived, worked and died in a community.
A street in Spitalfields whose Georgian terraced houses (dating from the early 18th century) survive as physical evidence of Huguenot prosperity and settlement.
A detailed survey of poverty and living conditions in London published by Charles Booth from 1889, using colour-coded maps to show wealth and deprivation street by street.
Victorian journalist and social researcher who documented the lives of London's working poor in the 1840s–1860s, providing detailed first-hand accounts of the East End's inhabitants.
A method of recording history through interviews with people who experienced events, providing personal testimony that written records do not capture.
